raw_case_text:
A 59-year-old male, non-smoker presented with increased cough and repeated episodes of moderate haemoptysis (60 mL/day) for three days. The patient was diagnosed with pulmonary tuberculosis and treated and cured 10 years ago with 'Category 1' anti-tubercular drugs (six-month regimen), later developing COPD with Bronchiectasis, thereby receiving long-term inhalational bronchodilators and corticosteroids. The patient also had occasional self-limiting episodes of 'mild' haemoptysis (~20 mL) for over three years. The patient was negative for viral markers pertinent to HIV, HCV, and HBV. An HRCT chest revealed a left upper lobe cavity with an intracavitary mass demonstrating 'air-crescent' sign, parenchymal destruction with peri-broncho-vascular interstitial thickening, dilated bronchi/bronchioles with ipsilateral lung volume reduction along with ground glass opacities, and adjacent pleural thickening (Figure 1). There was no evidence of mediastinal or hilar lymphadenopathy or pleural effusion.
A pulmonary function test showed a 'moderate' obstruction with a predicted FEV1 of 67% (GOLD 2024  grading) with no reversibility. Aspergillus fumigatus-specific IgG was positive. Bronchoalveolar lavage was negative for bacterial Gram staining, AFB smear, GeneXpert , conventional bacterial/mycobacterial cultures, and malignant cells but positive for galactomannan (OD=5.41). The presence of one host factor; use of 'long term' oral and inhalational corticosteroids, one clinical factor; positive 'air-crescent' sign on HRCT chest, and one microbiological factor; and positive BAL galactomannan collectively suggested the diagnosis of 'probable' invasive pulmonary aspergillosis as per the diagnosing criteria of EORTC/MSG  2020 (European Organization for Research and Treatment of Cancer and the Mycoses Study Group). However, serum galactomannan was not done.
The patient received intravenous voriconazole at a dose of 400 mg (~6 mg/kg), twice daily, following the diagnosis. Haemoptysis was refractory despite the appropriate antifungal therapy, given which the patient was taken up for left upper lobectomy. The post-operative period was uneventful. The patient was given chest physiotherapy, breathing exercises, and incentive spirometry practices. Chest radiography revealed adequate residual lung expansion following left upper lobectomy (Figure 2).
The surgical specimen tested negative for MTB GeneXpert  and AFB (MGIT) culture but demonstrated Aspergillus fumigatus on fungal culture, sensitive to voriconazole (microbroth dilution method). Histopathological examination of the resected lobe showed a markedly dilated and destroyed bronchial wall with septate hyphae invading the bronchial wall and peri-bronchial interstitium (Figure 3A). This confers the diagnosis of 'proven' invasive pulmonary aspergillosis. HPE also demonstrated peculiar, dense, diffuse infiltration of monomorphic neoplastic lymphocyte aggregates (Figure 3B) that were positive for both T cell and B cell markers with a Ki-67 proliferation index of 2%-4%, suggesting MALToma (Table 1).
Post-procedure was uneventful, with complete remission of symptoms. PET-CT scan (Figure 4) demonstrated lesions extending from the third to sixth rib, paravertebral, and chest muscles on the left side for which the Tumour Board's opinion was sought, suggesting chemotherapy. The patient, therefore, received oral chlorambucil (8 mg) at a 14 day-cycle every 28 days. After completion of six cycles of chemotherapy, the patient had complete remission of symptoms with no relapse of haemoptysis and has been on regular follow-up for the past year.

subjective.chief_complaint: A 59-year-old male non-smoker presented with a 3-day history of increased cough and repeated episodes of moderate hemoptysis (60 mL/day).
subjective.history_of_present_illness: The patient had experienced occasional self-limiting episodes of mild hemoptysis (~20 mL) for over 3 years and presented with an acute exacerbation of cough and moderate hemoptysis (60 mL/day) lasting 3 days.
subjective.past_medical_history: Pulmonary tuberculosis diagnosed and cured 10 years prior with a 6-month Category 1 anti-tubercular regimen; subsequently developed COPD and post-tubercular bronchiectasis managed with long-term inhaled bronchodilators and oral/inhaled corticosteroids. Lifetime non-smoker.
subjective.review_of_systems: Positive for chronic cough and acute-on-chronic moderate hemoptysis.

objective.routine_investigations: Viral serologies for HIV, HBV, and HCV were negative. Pulmonary function testing demonstrated moderate irreversible airflow obstruction with a predicted FEV1 of 67% (GOLD 2024 criteria). Postoperative chest radiograph showed adequate residual left lung expansion.
objective.advanced_workup: Chest HRCT demonstrated a left upper lobe cavity containing an intracavitary mass with a classic air-crescent sign, parenchymal destruction, peribronchovascular interstitial thickening, traction bronchiectasis, ipsilateral volume loss, ground-glass opacities, and adjacent pleural thickening without lymphadenopathy or pleural effusion. Serum Aspergillus fumigatus-specific IgG was positive. Bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) was strongly positive for galactomannan (OD 5.41) and negative for Gram stain, AFB smear, MTB GeneXpert, bacterial/mycobacterial cultures, and malignant cytology. Following left upper lobectomy for refractory hemoptysis, fungal culture of the resected lung grew voriconazole-susceptible Aspergillus fumigatus (negative for MTB GeneXpert and MGIT AFB culture), and histopathology confirmed proven invasive pulmonary aspergillosis (septate hyphae invading the destroyed bronchial wall and peribronchial interstitium) coexisting with pulmonary MALT lymphoma (monomorphic neoplastic lymphocyte aggregates positive for B- and T-cell markers, Ki-67 2%-4%). Postoperative PET-CT showed left 3rd-6th rib, paravertebral, and chest wall involvement.

assessment_and_plan.assessment_and_confirmation: Proven invasive pulmonary aspergillosis (Aspergillus fumigatus) arising in a post-tubercular left upper lobe cavity coexisting with primary pulmonary mucosa-associated lymphoid tissue lymphoma (MALToma), confirmed by HRCT air-crescent sign, positive serum A. fumigatus IgG, BAL galactomannan (OD 5.41), surgical tissue fungal culture, and lobectomy histopathology/immunohistochemistry. Treated with intravenous voriconazole (400 mg [~6 mg/kg] twice daily), left upper lobectomy for refractory hemoptysis, and 6 cycles of adjuvant oral chlorambucil (8 mg for 14 days every 28 days), achieving complete clinical remission without recurrent hemoptysis over 1 year of follow-up.
